title: Why a tidy home feels calmer
dek: A UCLA study listened to how people described their homes, then measured their stress hormones. The results are worth knowing.
imageAlt: Calm coastal living room in afternoon light

finding.label: working parents gave video tours of their own homes for the study

body.text: Most of us know the feeling. You walk in after work, see the pile on the bench and the washing on the chair, and something in you tightens. Researchers at UCLA wanted to know if that feeling shows up in the body.
What the researchers did

Darby Saxbe and Rena Repetti asked 60 people from dual-income families with children to give a video tour of their home and talk about it. Software counted the words they used. Some people described their homes with words like cluttered, messy and unfinished. Others used restful and natural words. Over the next three weekdays, the researchers tracked each person's mood and measured cortisol, a hormone the body uses to manage stress.
What they found

Women who described their homes as more cluttered and unfinished had flatter cortisol patterns across the day. In healthy people, cortisol is high in the morning and falls steadily, and a flatter pattern is linked with chronic stress. These women also felt more low as the day went on. Women who described their homes as restful showed the opposite: a healthier cortisol curve and a mood that improved through the evening.
For many people, home is meant to be where the body recovers from the day. A cluttered space can make that recovery harder.
What it does not say

This was a small study, and it found the link in wives, not husbands. It shows a connection, not proof that clutter causes stress. Many things affect cortisol. Still, it matches what a lot of people feel, and it suggests that a calm, finished home is more than a nice-to-have.
What helps

items: Clear one surface you see first when you walk in, such as the kitchen bench.
Keep a short daily reset of ten minutes, shared by everyone at home.
Hand off the deep, repetitive work, like bathrooms and floors, so your time at home is for rest.

sources.label: Saxbe and Repetti (2010). No Place Like Home: Home Tours Correlate With Daily Patterns of Mood and Cortisol. Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin.

cta: Come home to a finished house

title: Clutter and focus: what the brain science says
dek: Princeton neuroscientists found that the things around you compete for your brain's attention, even when you try to ignore them.
imageAlt: Clear marble kitchen island in a bright coastal home

finding.label: thing at a time: the visual system has limited capacity, so extra objects compete for it

body.text: If you work from home, your kitchen table may also be your desk. So it is fair to ask: does the mess around you affect how well you think?
The study

Stephanie McMains and Sabine Kastner at the Princeton Neuroscience Institute used brain scans to watch how the visual cortex handles several objects at once. Their 2011 paper in the Journal of Neuroscience shows that objects in view compete for the brain's limited processing capacity. Each one partly suppresses the others.

Attention can push back against that competition, but it takes effort. Professor Kastner has explained the practical point in plain terms: visual clutter competes with your ability to pay attention, and tidying your workspace can help you focus.
What it means at home

The study was done in a laboratory with simple shapes, not in kitchens. But the principle is simple. Fewer things in view means less for your brain to filter out. A clear bench or desk is one less demand on a mind that already has a full day.

items: Keep the surface you work at clear, not just tidy.
Put away what you are not using in the next hour.
Let regular cleaning keep the background calm, so you only have to manage the foreground.

sources.label: McMains and Kastner (2011). Interactions of Top-Down and Bottom-Up Mechanisms in Human Visual Cortex. Journal of Neuroscience.
Princeton Alumni Weekly. Psychology: Your Attention, Please.

cta: Clear the background, keep your focus

title: Buying time, not things
dek: A study of more than 6,000 people across four countries found that paying to skip chores you dislike is linked to a happier life.
imageAlt: Timber deck with a view over the coast

finding.label: adults in the US, Canada, Denmark and the Netherlands were surveyed

body.text: Many people feel a little guilty about paying for a cleaner. It can feel like an indulgence. Research led by Ashley Whillans, then at the University of British Columbia and now at Harvard Business School, suggests it is closer to a smart use of money.
What the research found

The team surveyed more than 6,000 adults in the United States, Canada, Denmark and the Netherlands. People who spent money to save time, for example on cleaning or other chores, reported greater life satisfaction. This held across income levels, not only for wealthy people.

To test cause and effect, the researchers also ran an experiment with working adults in Vancouver. On one weekend, people spent 40 dollars on something that saved them time. On another, they spent it on a material purchase. After the time-saving weekend, people felt less time pressure and more positive emotion.
People who hire a housecleaner might feel like they are being lazy. The research suggests buying time has similar benefits for happiness as having more money.
Why most people still don't do it
The surprise in the study was how few people choose this. When asked how they would spend a windfall, very few working adults chose to buy time. Guilt and habit get in the way.
A useful question
Instead of asking whether you can justify a cleaner, ask what the hours would be worth to you. A morning at the beach, a slower dinner with family, or simply a Saturday with nothing on the list.

sources.label: Whillans, Dunn, Smeets, Bekkers and Norton (2017). Buying time promotes happiness. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.
University of British Columbia via ScienceDaily (2017). Using money to buy time linked to increased happiness.

title: Clean sheets and a better night's sleep
dek: Most people say they sleep more comfortably in fresh bedding. Here is what the poll found, and what it does not prove.
imageAlt: Freshly made bed with clean linen

finding.label: of people in a US sleep poll said they get a more comfortable night's sleep on fresh sheets

body.text: There is a reason hotel beds feel good. The National Sleep Foundation's Bedroom Poll asked people about their bedrooms and how they sleep.
What people said

In the poll, 73 percent said they get a more comfortable night's sleep on sheets with a fresh scent, and 78 percent said fresh sheets make them more excited to go to bed. People who made their beds every day or almost every day were also more likely to say they slept well.
A fair caveat

This was a self-reported opinion poll, not a sleep experiment, and it was funded by a laundry brand. It tells us how people feel, not how many extra minutes of sleep they get. But how you feel about getting into bed matters for winding down.
What helps

items: Change and wash sheets every week.
Keep a second set so the bed is never left bare.
Make the bed each morning. It takes two minutes and the poll suggests it is worth it.

body.text: When we clean, we change bed linen you leave out for us, so you come home to a made bed.

sources.label: National Sleep Foundation. Bedroom Poll, Summary of Findings.

cta: Come home to a made bed

title: Dust mites in coastal homes: a guide for the Illawarra
dek: Australia's allergy specialists say dust mites are the most common allergen in humid coastal towns. Here is what actually reduces them.
imageAlt: Bright stone bathroom with natural light

finding.label: hot wash for bedding, every week, is the main advice from Australia's allergy specialists

body.text: Living near the ocean has many benefits. Humidity is not one of them. The Australasian Society of Clinical Immunology and Allergy (ASCIA), the peak body for allergy specialists, notes that house dust mites are the most common allergen source in humid areas such as coastal cities and towns.
For people with asthma, hay fever or eczema, dust mites can be a trigger. They cannot be removed completely, but their numbers and the allergen they produce can be reduced.
What ASCIA recommends

items: Wash sheets, pillowcases and other bedding every week in hot water above 60°C.
Vacuum carpets every week. Vacuuming briefly raises allergen in the air, so people with allergies can ask someone else to do it and stay out of the room for about 20 minutes.
Damp dust or use electrostatic cloths on hard surfaces, including hard floors, every week.
Keep the house dry and well ventilated to reduce humidity.

body.text: Where regular cleaning fits

Most of the advice comes down to doing the basics thoroughly and on a schedule. That is exactly what a regular clean is. If someone in your home has allergies, tell us and we will plan your visits around it.
This article is general information, not medical advice. If you or your child has asthma or allergies, talk to your doctor.

sources.label: ASCIA. Allergen Minimisation, Frequently Asked Questions.

cta: Book regular cleaning for allergy season

title: The invisible job: the mental load of running a home
dek: Housework is not only the scrubbing. It is the noticing, planning and remembering. New ABS data shows who carries it.
imageAlt: Hands typing on a laptop at a kitchen table

finding.label: average unpaid work a day for Australian women in 2024, compared with 3h 52m for men (ABS)

body.text: The Australian Bureau of Statistics released its latest Time Use Survey in August 2026. It shows that unpaid work, which includes housework, cooking, shopping and care, still takes a large part of every day.
The numbers

In 2024, Australian women spent an average of 4 hours 53 minutes a day on unpaid work, and men spent 3 hours 52 minutes. More than a third of women (36 percent) and 30 percent of men said they always or often felt rushed or pressed for time.
The part nobody sees

Sociologist Allison Daminger studied what she calls cognitive labour: anticipating what the household needs, working out the options, deciding, and then checking that it happened. In her 2019 study of 35 couples, published in the American Sociological Review, women did more of this work overall, especially the anticipating and the monitoring.
Noticing that the bathroom needs doing is a job in itself. So is remembering to book someone to do it.
Taking a task off the list for good

A regular clean with the same familiar team removes more than the scrubbing. Once your home plan is set, nobody has to notice, remind or organise. It simply happens, every week or fortnight, the same way.

sources.label: Australian Bureau of Statistics (2026). How Australians Use Their Time, 2024.
Daminger (2019). The Cognitive Dimension of Household Labor. American Sociological Review.

cta: Take cleaning off the mental list
